reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Posterior heel pain from inflammation of the bursa between the calcaneus and the Achilles tendon insertion
Often associated with insertional Achilles tendinopathy and with a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal process (Haglund deformity)
Tenderness is anterior to the Achilles tendon on either side of its insertion, distinguishing it from mid-portion tendinopathy
Aggravated by ankle dorsiflexion and by footwear pressure on the heel counter
Can occur in inflammatory arthropathies such as the spondyloarthritides, so consider systemic causes in bilateral or atypical presentations
Ultrasound or MRI shows bursal fluid and any associated insertional tendinopathy or bony prominence

Management is load and footwear modification, heel lift or shoe changes to reduce pressure, and physiotherapy; corticosteroid injection is used cautiously given proximity to the Achilles and rupture risk
reference.pathophysiology: The retrocalcaneal bursa sits between the posterosuperior calcaneus and the Achilles tendon. Repetitive compression and friction during ankle dorsiflexion, often aggravated by a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity (Haglund deformity) and by rigid heel counters, inflame the bursa. It commonly coexists with insertional Achilles tendinopathy, the two forming part of a posterior heel overload picture. Inflammatory arthropathies such as the spondyloarthritides can also produce a genuine inflammatory bursitis and enthesitis at this site.
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound to show bursal fluid and assess the Achilles insertion
MRI to characterise bursitis, insertional tendinopathy and bone oedema
Lateral radiograph to assess a Haglund prominence and insertional calcification
Inflammatory markers and HLA-B27 with rheumatological review if spondyloarthropathy is suspected
Clinical localisation of tenderness anterior to the tendon
redFlags: Features of inflammatory arthropathy such as bilateral heel pain, inflammatory back pain or other enthesitis
Sudden posterior pain and weakness suggesting Achilles rupture
Focal bone pain suggesting a calcaneal stress fracture
reference.prognosis: Usually improves with footwear and load modification and rehabilitation; cases linked to a Haglund deformity or insertional tendinopathy can be persistent and occasionally require surgery.
pitfalls: Corticosteroid injection near the Achilles with its attendant rupture risk
Confusing bursitis with mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy and mistreating it
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Modify activity and load, reducing aggravating ankle dorsiflexion and impact to allow the bursa to settle
Adjust footwear to remove pressure from a rigid heel counter and add a heel lift to offload the insertion
Undertake structured physiotherapy with Achilles stretching and eccentric loading for coexisting insertional tendinopathy
Trial simple analgesia or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain, using intrabursal corticosteroid only with caution given the risk of Achilles rupture
Screen for spondyloarthritis in bilateral or atypical disease and refer for rheumatological assessment and disease-modifying therapy
Consider surgery, such as calcaneal osteotomy for a Haglund deformity with bursal excision or debridement, for refractory cases
